He admits to regrettable sales early on but decided never to repeat them. In the long run, scientifically grounded practices plus good arguments naturally earn trust.

8:14 Outsiders don't get taken advantage of and dare to challenge assumptions
David's parents lived through the Great Depression and always considered themselves outsiders to the capital markets, afraid of being taken advantage of by insiders, so they never invested. But he points out that the financial science of the 60s and 70s boiled down to two points: long-term returns on stocks and bonds meet expectations, and professional fund managers underperform the market after fees. These two points made it clear to outsiders that public markets are fair to everyone. The outsider mindset also brings a benefit: a willingness to challenge assumptions. The scholars who changed finance back then were also outsiders because they had data, making conclusions that Wall Street hated hard to refute.

22:29 Index funds are a product of marketing genius, not scientific conclusion
David emphasizes distinguishing between passive management and index funds. He notes that the most important change in the financial industry from the 20th century to today is the shift to passive management, but index funds are a product of marketing genius, not something a scientist would conclude. A scientist would not impose the constraint of 'must track an index' on a portfolio, because constraints have an economic cost. Indices themselves are human-managed portfolios; for example, the S&P 500 is not strictly the top 500 companies, and inclusions and exclusions involve judgment. Dimensional considers itself passive, not indexed.

31:34 The cost of trading at the closing price is paying 4% more
When a stock is added to the S&P 500, index funds must buy at the closing price on that day. David says you can ask your broker to guarantee execution at the closing price, but the cost is 'willing to pay any price.' When all S&P 500 managers do this simultaneously, they push the stock price up by an average of 4% above fair value. It's like a three-card monte game: investors think they're not paying transaction costs, but the 4% premium reverts the next day. This is the hidden cost of index funds and a reason passive managers can do better.

35:37 Investors in 1971 had it an order of magnitude worse than today
Asked whether he'd rather be an investor in 1971 or today, David unhesitatingly chose today. In 1971, management fees were as high as 1-2% per year, and NYSE-set commission rates were an order of magnitude higher than today, even 10-20 times higher; to absorb these high commissions, institutions spawned the 'soft dollar' industry, similar to paying a high ticket price for double miles. Custody costs were also high, with some banks still keeping handwritten ledgers. In contrast, today's fees and transparency give ordinary investors a much fairer deal.

40:41 Research is a public good; the gap lies in execution
David points out that financial science has become public knowledge, especially since Fama and French insisted on making their research public, but competitors' new research may not be peer-reviewed. He believes that with thousands of professors repeatedly mining the same data over decades, it's unlikely there will be a disruptive new result. The real difference lies in implementation: Myron Scholes said, 'Ideas are cheap; execution matters.' Execution is not just placing orders; it includes the engineering of portfolio construction. Ken French treats execution as engineering; always buying at the ask and selling at the bid in trading accumulates losses over time, which is why Dimensional developed fine trading techniques.

51:54 10% annual return isn't magic; it's people refusing to sit still
David explains why stocks return about 10% annually over the long term: it's not magic, but humanity's instinct to improve life. In the early days of the pandemic, U.S. stocks fell about 30%; he told clients he didn't know what would happen, but he believed companies would not sit still—they would innovate, shut down, pivot—and the recession lasted only one quarter. This is also why one should hold the market portfolio rather than individual stocks—individual stocks can go to zero, but the market won't. Holding the market portfolio is a bet on the overall economy and the human creativity within it.

1:14:29 No matter how hot private markets get, it's not worth leaving your comfort zone
Pressed on his view of private markets, David says bluntly, 'I'm not tempted.' He likes the transparency of public markets: listed companies must disclose a lot of information, there is price discovery many times a day, liquidity is always available, and tax reporting is timely. He says he already has a strategy he considers fair and doesn't want to leave his comfort zone for something unfamiliar. He even says that if he were an advisor, he would allow clients to play with 10% of their money in individual stocks, private equity, or venture capital, but the remaining 90% must follow a rigorous process.

item.title: What the Fed fears most is not tariffs but unanchored inflation expectations
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-masterscale-通胀预期失锚-美联储最怕的不是关税/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-masterscale-通胀预期失锚-美联储最怕的不是关税/
item.description: Chicago Fed President Goolsbee identifies the biggest risk as inflation: after five and a half years above target, the AI narrative may push rates up in the short term rather than down; his key advice for rate-sensitive industries is to watch the data, not the stock market.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Fed President Goolsbee identifies the biggest risk as inflation: after five and a half years above target, the AI narrative may push rates up in the short term rather than down; his key advice for rate-sensitive industries is to watch the data, not the stock market.

A frontline policymaker rarely offers actionable quantitative anchors: the terminal rate is roughly 3%, but only if inflation returns to 2%; he also offers contrarian takes on the AI bubble and job-loss panic.

4:15 19 chairs are not for consensus but for argument
He explains why the FOMC is worth keeping with 12 regional Fed presidents plus 7 Board governors, totaling 19 chairs: not for consensus, but to let different worldviews collide under high uncertainty. Goolsbee says colleagues can shout at him and can change his interpretation of data. This structure insulates rate decisions from the political cycle as much as possible, because the 14-year staggered terms mean no one can replace the whole table at once. The direct lesson for founders: when making major judgments, surround yourself with people who dare to push back, not an echo chamber.

9:25 The Fed's real fear is not price hikes but unanchored expectations
The real danger of tariff and oil price shocks is not a one-time price increase but making people believe high inflation will persist. Once such expectations form, workers demand 6% wages, businesses price at 7%, and the Fed must use a deep recession to break expectations if it wants to bring inflation down. Goolsbee calls this 'unanchoring of inflation expectations' and says it is the self-fulfilling mechanism he is most vigilant about. For entrepreneurs, this logic means: whether a cost increase is one-off matters more than how much costs rise.

10:31 Five and a half years above target, the Fed's own record is not pretty
Goolsbee admits the Fed's performance has not been pretty: nearly six years, at least five and a half of them above the 2% target, with a recent reversal in the past year. He cites on-the-ground observations from the Seventh District (Midwest): businesses say input costs have surged, farmers say selling prices are not rising but costs are crushing, and everyone talks about affordability. His conclusion: with the public highly sensitive to prices, any new supply shock—tariffs, Middle East oil prices, chip shortages, AI data centers—is more likely to be interpreted as long-term inflation.

14:44 The new chair is pulling back the Fed's forward guidance
New Chair Kevin Walsh is overhauling the Fed's communication style: he dislikes 'forward guidance'—the explicit promise that 'if X happens, we will hike or cut.' Goolsbee observes that FOMC statements have become noticeably shorter, and Walsh has set up five working groups covering inflation, AI and productivity, the balance sheet, and other areas, staffed with well-known people he trusts. Reports are not out yet, but they could become Walsh's signature reform. Markets must adapt: the Fed will make fewer promises, and future expectation volatility may be higher.

20:34 Replacing people to influence rates is the red line for independence
Goolsbee divides today's pressures into two types: personal attacks on Powell, Lisa Cook, and others, including criminal investigations and attempts to remove them; and direct demands to 'cut rates.' He says the Fed's independence has traditionally been narrowly defined—setting rates without political interference. Once an administration tries to influence rates by replacing people, 'any economist would see that as a problem.' He does not go all the way, but this is his clearest statement to the White House.

25:00 AI is a reason to hike rates in the short term, not cut them
He first cools the AI narrative with district facts: manufacturing has the highest share in the entire Fed system, but companies are still looking for use cases and complaining that tokens are too expensive; productivity growth, after a two-and-a-half-year pickup, has shown about six months of weakness. Then he offers a counterintuitive judgment: if everyone simultaneously pours money into data centers, betting with IPOs or expected future earnings, the short-term economy will overheat. The central bank's daily job is to prevent overheating, not to judge whether AI will revolutionize things in 20 years, so AI's short-term policy implication may be to push rates up, not down.

28:26 AI taking all jobs is the lump of labor fallacy
He attributes the narrative that 'AI will make everyone unemployed' to the lump of labor fallacy: treating the total amount of labor as a fixed stone that, once AI surpasses it, leaves no new jobs for people. He says this claim has been proven wrong every time in the past; he admits 'maybe this time is different,' but he is willing to bet the opposite: in 20 years there will not be 95% unemployment, nor will only six people own all AI companies. He positions himself as a 'grim optimist'—not shying away from short-term pain but optimistic about long-term income growth.

35:00 The terminal rate is roughly 3%, provided inflation turns around
Goolsbee offers a rare quantitative anchor: his personal loose view is that if inflation returns to a 2% path, rates will converge to the neutral rate (what he calls star), roughly 3% nominal rate = 2% inflation + 1% real rate. But the precondition is that inflation must turn downward; the past five and a half years have been above target, and the last year has been moving in the wrong direction. For rate-sensitive industries, his advice is to watch data and inflation, not the stock market—the people around the FOMC table discuss the real economy, and the stock market is only a secondary reference.

item.title: Sunscreen Toxicity Myth Debunked: Entering Blood Isn't Harmful, but Vitamin D Risk Is Real
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-sciencevs-防晒霜不是毒药-但深肤色人群可能真不用防黑素瘤/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-27-sciencevs-防晒霜不是毒药-但深肤色人群可能真不用防黑素瘤/
item.description: The most-cited evidence for 'sunscreen is toxic and causes cancer' mostly involves absurd doses or reversed causality; chemical sunscreen entering the blood doesn't equal toxicity. But daily application does increase the risk of vitamin D deficiency in winter, and evidence for preventing melanoma in darker skin is especially weak.
item.content:encoded:
The most-cited evidence for 'sunscreen is toxic and causes cancer' mostly involves absurd doses or reversed causality; chemical sunscreen entering the blood doesn't equal toxicity. But daily application does increase the risk of vitamin D deficiency in winter, and evidence for preventing melanoma in darker skin is especially weak.

This episode checks the three most widespread scare claims on social media against the original studies, so you can learn which are cases of dose determining toxicity and which are real trade-offs. High information density, no cherry-picking.

6:52 The anti-sunscreen flagship experiment used doses equivalent to centuries of human use
The 2001 rat study most often cited by anti-sunscreen rhetoric: female rats fed oxybenzone developed enlarged uteruses, interpreted as endocrine disruption. But Brandon Adler points out the rats ingested it, and the dose translates to a human using oxybenzone sunscreen continuously for 35–277 years. This is a classic case of 'the dose makes the poison': the experimental exposure is completely incomparable to real-world use.

10:00 Blood absorption being called poisoning misreads the FDA threshold
In the FDA's maximal-use trial, sunscreen was applied to 75% of body surface for 4–5 consecutive days; oxybenzone was detected in blood and exceeded an FDA threshold, and the internet immediately said 'sunscreen is toxic.' But that threshold doesn't indicate harm; the FDA's own conclusion was 'these findings do not suggest that individuals should refrain from using sunscreen.' A systematic review of about 30 studies also found no clear evidence that oxybenzone affects hormones at normal use levels.

14:10 Coral bleaching is a climate problem, not a sunscreen problem
Oxybenzone has been banned in Hawaii and elsewhere due to coral bleaching concerns. In the lab, soaking juvenile corals in chemical sunscreen is indeed toxic and causes bleaching; but concentrations measured in real seawater are far lower. Research repeatedly confirms that the primary cause of coral bleaching is climate change, with sunscreen at most 'adding insult to injury,' not the main driver. After consumer backlash, many manufacturers have already voluntarily removed oxybenzone.

17:31 Homemade sunscreen tested at SPF under 6
Some people make DIY sunscreen from zinc oxide and beef tallow, with an absurd logic: you first have to buy a commercial sunscreen containing zinc oxide to add tallow to. A study took 15 online recipes and tested them in the lab; several contained no UV-filtering ingredients at all, and the rest had SPF below 6, offering almost no protection. If you're worried about chemical sunscreen entering the blood, switch to mineral sunscreen, but don't DIY.

20:00 Newly approved chemical filters are too large to enter the blood
The FDA recently approved bemotrizinol, the first new chemical sunscreen ingredient in nearly 20 years, though it's been used in Europe and Australia for years. It's truly broad-spectrum, stable, and easy to formulate, and its large molecular size means it's poorly absorbed through skin, behaving more like a mineral sunscreen. For those concerned about ingredients entering the blood, this is a new option worth watching over older chemical filters.

29:20 Daily sunscreen raises winter vitamin D deficiency risk by 35%
Rachel Neale's team ran a 600-person randomized controlled trial: one group lived normally, the other applied SPF50 daily on days with UV index ≥3. After a year, summer vitamin D levels didn't drop in either group; the sunscreen group averaged only slightly lower. But by the end of winter, the sunscreen group had about a 35% higher risk of vitamin D deficiency than the control group. Because the body stores vitamin D in fat and releases it slowly, lower summer stores mean insufficient winter levels.

37:20 Sunscreen's evidence against squamous cell carcinoma is solid, but not yet for melanoma
A UK study of 400,000 people found 'people who use sunscreen are more likely to get skin cancer,' but the authors clarified this is reverse causation: those who use more sunscreen often spend more time outdoors, apply too little, or don't reapply. A cleaner Australian RCT with 1,600 people followed over 10 years found daily sunscreen reduced squamous cell carcinoma by about 40%; melanoma cases were 11 vs 22, showing a halved risk but not statistically significant due to too few cases.

43:40 Darker skin has built-in SPF15, so daily sunscreen isn't necessary
Adamson's systematic review found almost no data supporting a link between sun exposure and melanoma in non-whites: melanin moves to the skin's surface and acts as natural sunscreen, giving darker skin types an equivalent of SPF15+ protection. Australia updated its guidelines accordingly, saying the two darkest skin types don't need routine sunscreen for cancer prevention; the American AAD hasn't changed, and Adamson criticizes it as 'not science-based.' He still recommends sunscreen for everyone to prevent sunburn and photoaging, but not necessarily daily.
